1.title: An Exile's Date
1.context: Ezekiel was a priest deported to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, eleven years before Jerusalem fell. The River Kebar was likely a large irrigation canal near Nippur where Judean exiles were settled.
1.question: When your life is dated by a loss, like the fifth year of an exile, what do you still expect God to do there?

1.title: The Storm from the North
1.context: The four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings, belong to the vision's machinery and are never explained inside the chapter. Later chapters call these beings cherubim.
1.question: What do you make of a God whose arrival looks less like calm and more like a storm at war?

1.title: Wheels Within Wheels
1.context: The wheels move in any direction without turning, and the spirit of the creatures is in them. The text offers the picture without an interpretation, and interpreters have disagreed about its meaning ever since.
1.question: Where have you seen movement in your life that only later looked guided?

1.title: The Throne Above the Expanse
1.context: Above the expanse sits a throne, and on it a figure described through layers of likeness and appearance. The prophet keeps a careful distance in his language, as if the words themselves were not adequate.
1.question: How does it change your prayers to picture God enthroned above everything, rather than beside you at your level?

1.title: Facedown in the Dirt
1.context: The rainbow around the throne reaches back to Noah's sign after the flood. Ezekiel's response to the glory is the one he repeats at every sight of it: he falls facedown.
1.question: What is the honest physical response, tears, silence, falling down, that praise has ever drawn out of you?

2.title: Son of Man, Stand Up
2.context: Son of man is God's address to Ezekiel nearly a hundred times in this book. It means mortal, a human being, and in this book it is never the title of anyone else.
2.question: What steadies you when you are reminded, kindly or not, that you are only human?

2.title: Whether They Listen or Not
2.context: The commission defines success before the mission starts: the people will know a prophet has been among them, whether or not they obey him. Response is not the measure Ezekiel is given.
2.question: What work in your life needs to be judged by faithfulness rather than by results?

2.title: Briers, Thorns, and Scorpions
2.context: The audience is described in advance as rebellious, and the prophet is forbidden the natural response of fear or dismay. He is sent to speak God's words, not his own, whether they hear or refuse.
2.question: Whose reaction are you most tempted to manage, and what would you say if you only answered to the message?

2.title: Sweet as Honey
2.context: Eating a scroll was a sign act as much as a vision: the message had to be inside the messenger before it could come out of him. Its taste, sweet as honey, surprises in a book about judgment.
2.question: What hard word have you had to take in fully before you could pass it on truthfully?

2.title: A Forehead Like Flint
2.context: Tel-abib, where the exiles lived, sounds in Hebrew like both mound of the flood and mound of grain. Ezekiel arrives there not preaching but stunned, and sits among them seven days in silence.
2.question: When has sitting with people in their trouble, before saying anything, been the truest ministry you could offer?

3.title: Made a Watchman
3.context: A watchman stood on a city wall or tower to sound the trumpet at the approach of an army. His duty ended at the warning; what the city did with it was the city's responsibility.
3.question: What warning, to speak or to heed, are you currently carrying?

3.title: The Wicked Man's Blood
3.context: The charter is stark: the watchman who stays silent shares the guilt of the death he could have warned against, while the watchman who warns is cleared even if he is ignored.
3.question: Is there a hard conversation you have been treating as optional that this charter would call part of the job?

3.title: The Righteous Man Who Turns
3.context: The second case guards the other side: a righteous life is not a stored credit that covers a later turn. Both cases make the warning itself the watchman's whole account.
3.question: Where are you relying on past faithfulness to excuse a present drift?

3.title: The Glory Again, on the Plain
3.context: God takes Ezekiel out to the plain and shows him the same glory he saw at the river, as if the commission needed its vision repeated before the work began.
3.question: What truth do you need to hear a second time before you will act on it?

3.title: Bound and Silent in His House
3.context: Ezekiel's silence was itself a sign: he spoke only when God gave a word, so every oracle arrived marked as released, not improvised. Later chapters record his mouth opening for good on the night the city fell (33:22).
3.question: What would change in your speech if you treated your words as something to release carefully rather than constantly?

4.title: A City Drawn on a Brick
4.context: Clay bricks were everyday building material in Babylon, and an inscribed brick made a portable model of Jerusalem under siege. Sign acts like this were street theater meant to be watched and asked about.
4.question: What has God used in your ordinary surroundings to get your attention?

4.title: Three Hundred Ninety Days on One Side
4.context: The days correspond to years of sin, 390 for Israel and 40 for Judah, though interpreters differ over which periods they count. The prophet bears the sin symbolically, in his body, lying bound where the neighbors could see.
4.question: What burden have you carried in plain sight that nobody thought to ask you about?

4.title: Siege Bread, Weighed and Timed
4.context: Twenty shekels of food a day is roughly eight ounces, a starvation ration eaten at set times to picture famine discipline inside a besieged city. The mixed grains are the sweepings of an almost empty storehouse.
4.question: How do shortages, of food, time, or strength, expose what your household actually runs on?

4.title: A Third, a Third, a Third
4.context: The hair is weighed on scales and divided into exact thirds: burned, struck with the sword, and scattered to the wind, mapping pestilence, war, and exile. A few hairs tucked in the prophet's garment are the remnant in miniature.
4.question: Which third of the warning, burned, struck, or scattered, would your city most need to hear?

4.title: Worse Than the Nations
4.context: The interpretation charges Jerusalem with the book's most shocking comparison: surrounded by nations, she has rebelled more than they, judged by the standard she alone was given.
4.question: What standard have you been given, in faith or family, that makes your failures harder to excuse than other people's?

5.title: Set Your Face Toward the Mountains
5.context: The high places were local shrines on hills and under trees where Israel mixed the worship of the LORD with the rites of the surrounding nations. The first sermon is addressed to the land itself, its mountains, hills, ravines, and valleys.
5.question: What places in your life, habits, rooms, routines, carry a worship you would not defend out loud?

5.title: A Remnant in the Ruin
5.context: Even in the first judgment sermon, a remnant is promised: survivors among the nations who will remember and loathe their own sin. Repentance in exile, not escape from exile, is the door left open.
5.question: What have you only been able to see clearly about yourself from a distance, in exile from how things were?

5.title: The End Has Come
5.context: Chapter 7 is built like an alarm, with short hammering lines and the repeated announcement that the end has come upon the four corners of the land. Its poetry refuses to let the hearer treat the warning as background noise.
5.question: What alarm in your life have you learned to sleep through?

5.title: Silver in the Streets
5.context: In a siege, money fails first as a store of value: silver is thrown into the streets because it cannot be eaten. The oracle presses the point that wealth which cannot save becomes refuse at exactly the moment it is most needed.
5.question: If your money could not rescue you, what would you discover you had actually been trusting?

5.title: They Will Seek Peace and Find None
5.context: The closing picture is of guidance itself breaking down: vision fails from the prophet, instruction from the priest, counsel from the elders. A society can lose its bearings before it loses its walls.
5.question: When every trusted voice goes quiet, where do you turn for direction?

6.title: Taken by a Lock of Hair
6.context: The elders of Judah are sitting in Ezekiel's house in Babylon when the vision takes him six hundred miles to Jerusalem. The book dates it precisely: the sixth year of the exile, about a year after the scroll.
6.question: What room in your inner life have you been keeping closed to inspection?

6.title: The Idol That Provokes Jealousy
6.context: The first stop is an idol set up at the temple's own gate. Four times in the tour a refrain promises something still greater, so each room is judged against a worse one behind it.
6.question: Which of your compromises do you rate as the small one because you know a worse one exists?

6.title: Seventy Elders in the Dark
6.context: In a hidden chamber, seventy elders of Israel burn incense to images covering the walls, each man certain the LORD does not see him in the dark. Jaazaniah, named here, belonged to a leading Jerusalem family.
6.question: What do you do differently when you are sure no one who matters can see you?

6.title: Weeping for Tammuz
6.context: Tammuz was a Mesopotamian god whose yearly death and mourning filled a month named for him, a month that still bears his name in the Hebrew calendar. The women weeping for him are sitting at the temple's north gate.
6.question: Whose grief or devotion have you borrowed because it was in the air around you?

6.title: Faces to the East
6.context: The tour ends in the inner court with twenty-five men between the porch and the altar, backs to the sanctuary, faces to the sunrise, worshiping the sun in the house of the God who made it.
6.question: When has your worship faced the wrong direction while keeping all the right furniture?

7.title: Six Men with Weapons
7.context: The executioners enter from the Upper Gate, the direction of invasion. The vision is careful to name a seventh figure among them who carries no weapon at all, only a scribe's kit.
7.question: When judgment is moving through a place you love, what do you watch first, the weapons or the writing kit?

7.title: A Mark on the Forehead
7.context: The mark is the Hebrew letter tav, which in the script of that era was shaped like a cross or an X. It is given not to the impressive but to those who sigh and groan over what the city has become.
7.question: What marks a person as belonging to God here, if it is grief over sin rather than success or status?

7.title: Ah, Lord GOD, Will You Destroy Everyone?
7.context: Ezekiel's intercession is the first prayer of protest in the book, and God does not rebuke him for it. The answer is not mercy withdrawn but guilt named: the land is full of bloodshed, and the city full of injustice.
7.question: What have you argued with God about that you were afraid was unbelief, and turned out to be intercession?

7.title: Coals Between the Wheels
7.context: The man in linen goes twice: first to mark, then to carry fire. The cherubim and wheels reappear under the temple, and the vision now names the creatures of chapter 1 outright.
7.question: Where has the same presence that once protected a place become, by slow degrees, the presence that judges it?

7.title: The Glory Moves to the East Gate
7.context: The departure happens in stages, threshold to east gate to the mountain east of the city, as if the glory pauses at each step. What Ezekiel watches leave is the same living throne he fell before at the canal.
7.question: What slow departures, in a church, a family, a life, have you only recognized after the last stage?

8.title: We Are the Meat in This Pot
8.context: The leaders' proverb was a boast disguised as a jingle: the city is the pot and they are the meat, safe inside while the exiles are the discarded cuts. Pelatiah, named in the vision, dies in it as the word is spoken.
8.question: What saying does your group repeat that makes it feel safe for the wrong reason?

8.title: You Will Not Be the Meat
8.context: God turns the proverb inside out: the real meat in the pot is the leaders' own victims, and the leaders themselves will be dragged out to the border and judged there. The boast becomes the sentence.
8.question: What has a slogan of yours cost the people it was never about?

8.title: A Little Sanctuary in the Countries
8.context: The promise is addressed past Jerusalem to the people both cities counted as refuse. God calls Himself their sanctuary in exile, a smaller and portable holiness, but His own presence all the same.
8.question: Where has God been a little sanctuary for you in a season that looked like pure loss?

8.title: One Heart, Taken Out in Stone
8.context: The new heart promise appears here first, aimed at returning exiles: the heart of stone removed, a heart of flesh given, so that obedience becomes possible from the inside. Chapter 36 will take the same promise much further.
8.question: What would you ask God to change in you that effort and advice have never reached?

8.title: The Glory Settles on the Mountain
8.context: The glory's last stop in the vision is the Mount of Olives, east of the city, where it stands rather than vanishes. Ezekiel comes out of the vision and simply reports everything to the exiles sitting with him.
8.question: What have you been shown that your only assignment, for now, is to report faithfully?

9.title: Baggage by Day, a Hole by Dusk
9.context: Exile baggage was what a deportee could carry: a few clothes, tools, and food for the road. Ezekiel performs the sign in daylight and repeats the exit at twilight, digging through the mud-brick wall of his own house.
9.question: What is the thing you own that you would pack first if everything else had to be left?

9.title: The Prince with His Face Covered
9.context: The prince is Zedekiah, Jerusalem's last king. The sign foretells his night flight, his capture, and his journey to a Babylon he would never see; 2 Kings 25 records that his eyes were put out before the journey.
9.question: Where are you planning an escape route from something God has already addressed?

9.title: Bread with Trembling
9.context: The second sign is at the table: eating and drinking with visible fear, the daily bread of a city that knows the siege is coming. Ordinary acts become prophecy when the prophet performs them.
9.question: What does your eating, spending, or sleeping say about what you actually expect?

9.title: The Days Are Lengthened
9.context: The first proverb is a shrug set to rhyme in Hebrew: days lengthen, visions fail. It borrows the form of folk wisdom to excuse unbelief, and God answers it with a proverb of His own about nearness.
9.question: What true thing have you heard so often, and waited on so long, that it has started to sound false?

9.title: Not for Distant Times
9.context: The second proverb grants the prophecy and only postpones it, visions for distant times. God's answer closes the chapter by removing delay itself from the hearers' excuses.
9.question: What have you filed under someday that has quietly become a never?

10.title: Prophets of Their Own Imagination
10.context: The charge against the false prophets is not first that they lied, but that they followed their own spirit and saw nothing. A message manufactured at home can sound like prophecy and still be only the prophet's own weather.
10.question: How do you test whether a confident spiritual word, including your own, came from God or from imagination?

10.title: Whitewash on a Flimsy Wall
10.context: Whitewash was a thin plaster coating that made a wall look finished. The storm God describes, rain, hailstones, and wind, is the kind of weather that finds out what a wall is actually made of.
10.question: What in your life looks finished from the street and unproven in a storm?

10.title: Charms on Every Wrist
10.context: The prophetesses sewed charms and veils used in hunting souls, declaring life and death for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread. The oracle promises to tear the charms off and free the people they snared.
10.question: What small payments, flattery, approval, comfort, have bought spiritual words you wanted to hear?

10.title: Idols in the Heart, Stumbling Blocks in the Face
10.context: The elders come to inquire while carrying idols in their hearts, and God says He will answer them Himself, in person, according to the idol they bring. A consultation can become a judgment when the heart arrives pre-decided.
10.question: What question have you brought to God with the answer already chosen?

10.title: Noah, Daniel, and Job
10.context: The three names span the whole Bible as Ezekiel knew it: Noah the ancient righteous, Job the sufferer of the wisdom books, and Daniel, whom this book names again later. Even they, God says, would save only themselves.
10.question: Whose righteousness have you been hoping to borrow, parent, pastor, spouse, instead of standing on your own?

11.title: What Is Vine Wood Good For?
11.context: Grapevine wood is too soft and crooked for timber, pegs, or tools; its whole value is in its fruit. The short parable sets up the long one: a vine that stops bearing has no second use to fall back on.
11.question: What is the one fruit your life is actually for, underneath all the useful things you also do?

11.title: A Baby in Her Own Blood
11.context: The foundling picture is drawn from real custom: an unwanted newborn could be exposed and left, unwashed, cord uncut. Jerusalem's story starts not with her beauty but with the passersby who did nothing, and the One who did.
11.question: What part of your story began with being utterly unwanted or overlooked, and who passed by and stopped?

11.title: I Spread My Cloak Over You
11.context: The cloak spread over her is a marriage act, the same gesture Ruth will ask of Boaz. Everything that follows, the washing, oil, embroidered clothes, jewelry, and fame among the nations, is given before it is earned, because it is not earned at all.
11.question: What have you received from God that you later started treating as your own achievement?

11.title: She Trusted in Her Beauty
11.context: The betrayal is told at story level in the text's own terms: the gifts themselves, gold, clothing, food, even children, are carried to the lovers and the shrines. The chapter refuses to let the reader look away from the pattern of gift turned against giver.
11.question: What gift in your life is most at risk of funding the very thing that would ruin you?

11.title: Remember, and Be Ashamed
11.context: The judgment runs its full legal course, and then the chapter does the unthinkable: God remembers His covenant anyway, gives Jerusalem her worse sisters as daughters, and aims the whole history at a shame that ends in atonement, not destruction.
11.question: What memory of your own failure has God turned into humility rather than a life sentence?

12.title: A Riddle of Two Eagles
12.context: The riddle is a nature story with the names filed off: a great eagle, a cedar top carried to a city of merchants, a vine that stretches its roots toward a second eagle. Politically literate hearers would have decoded it before the explanation came.
12.question: What story is God telling in the events around you that you have been refusing to decode?

12.title: The King Who Rebelled
12.context: The first eagle is Nebuchadnezzar, who took Jehoiachin to Babylon and set his uncle Zedekiah on the throne as a vassal. The vine's turn toward Egypt was Zedekiah's rebellion, shopping for a second patron while under oath to the first.
12.question: Where are you quietly reaching for a second rescuer while bound by a commitment to the first?

12.title: My Oath That He Despised
12.context: Treason against Babylon was, in Babylon's courts, a political crime; God calls it something else. The oath Zedekiah swore was sworn in God's name, so breaking faith with Nebuchadnezzar was breaking faith with God Himself.
12.question: What promise have you been treating as merely practical that was, in fact, sacred?

12.title: I Myself Will Plant It
12.context: The tender sprig is a shoot from the same cedar the first eagle cropped. God plants it Himself, on Israel's high mountain, and birds of every kind nest in it; no human king in the story plants anything that lasts.
12.question: What is growing in your life that you cannot claim credit for, and how do you tend something that is not yours?

12.title: All the Trees Will Know
12.context: The last verse states the book's whole theology of history in four reversals: high tree lowered, low tree raised, green tree dried, dry tree flourishing. Every empire in the surrounding chapters is an illustration of this single verse.
12.question: Which of the four reversals are you living in right now, and what does it ask of you?

13.title: The Sour Grapes Proverb
13.context: The proverb blamed the fathers' sins for the children's teeth: a tidy explanation that made the exiles victims of history and excused them from repentance. God bans the saying in Israel and replaces it with a sentence about individual souls.
13.question: What explanation of your trouble works mostly to excuse you from changing?

13.title: The Righteous Man
13.context: The first generation is sketched as a checklist of refusals and generosities: no idolatry, no adultery, no oppression, debts returned, the hungry fed, the naked clothed. Righteousness here is mostly what a man will not touch and what he will not keep.
13.question: Which item on that list, a refusal or a generosity, is the live one for you this week?

13.title: The Violent Son
13.context: The son grows up inside a righteous house and chooses the opposite of everything in it. The case is built to break the proverb from the other side: a good father is no more a guarantee than a bad one is a curse.
13.question: What are you carrying, guilt or credit, for an adult child's choices that were never yours to make?

13.title: The Grandson Who Saw and Refused
13.context: The third generation sees all his father's sins and does not do them, proving the chain can break in either direction. The audience's objection follows immediately, because a doctrine this fair feels unfair to people who preferred the proverb.
13.question: Where can a chain break in your family because you saw clearly and chose otherwise?

13.title: Do I Take Any Pleasure?
13.context: The chapter ends not with the defendant but with the Judge, who states under oath that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The demand that follows, repent and live, is paired with a command to get a new heart, months before chapter 36 explains who gives it.
13.question: What would you do differently this week if you believed God was arguing for your life, not against it?

14.title: The Lioness and Her First Cub
14.context: The lament is a qinah, a funeral dirge, sung over kings still alive when it was written. The first cub is generally understood as Jehoahaz, taken to Egypt in chains after a three-month reign, though the poem names no names.
14.question: What are you already grieving that has not technically ended yet?

14.title: The Second Cub, Caged with Hooks
14.context: The lioness raises another cub when the first hope fails, and the nations set on him with hooks and a cage, the standard way of transporting captured kings. Most readers hear Jehoiachin here, and some hear Zedekiah approaching.
14.question: What second hope have you raised in the same pattern that consumed the first?

14.title: A Vine Fit for a Scepter
14.context: The poem changes animals mid-song: the mother becomes a vine whose strong branches were fit for scepters, and the fire that finishes it starts from its own main branch. Judah's ruin is pictured as self-kindled as much as invaded.
14.question: Where has the damage in your life come out of your own strongest branch?

14.title: Fire Against the Forest of the South
14.context: This short oracle stands at the end of chapter 20 in the English ordering of the text, though some printings number it as the start of chapter 21. Its fire does not sort green trees from dry, a line the New Testament later quotes about Jerusalem.
14.question: What have you assumed would be spared in a judgment because it was green and growing?

14.title: Just Telling Parables
14.context: The complaint is the prophet's most human line: his audience has learned to enjoy the performance and miss the message. God's answer, which the next episode takes up, abandons pictures for a straight historical record.
14.question: When did you last receive a hard word as entertainment, a good sermon, a good story, and walk away unchanged?

15.title: I Will Not Be Consulted by You
15.context: The date is the seventh year of the exile, and the elders' inquiry is refused before it is heard. Instead of an answer about the future, they are made to sit through their fathers' whole record of rebellion.
15.question: What question would you rather God answered instead of the history He keeps bringing up?

15.title: The Day I Chose Israel
15.context: The retelling starts in Egypt and starts with rebellion: on the very day of choosing, the chosen refuse to throw away their idols. God's restraint is explained by one motive only, repeated through the chapter, the sake of His name among the nations watching.
15.question: What has God's reputation, rather than your deserving, protected in your life?

15.title: The Wilderness, Twice
15.context: Two wilderness generations refuse the same gifts, life-giving ordinances and the Sabbath as a sign, and twice the sentence of dying in the desert is held back by the same motive. The gift they reject is described as the thing that would have made them live.
15.question: What gift from God have you been treating as a burden because accepting it would arrange your life?

15.title: Like the Families of the Lands
15.context: The indictment lands on the men sitting in the room: the fathers' pattern has become the sons' ambition, to be like the nations, serving wood and stone. God announces He will be king over them whether they crown Him or not.
15.question: What version of being like everyone else still tempts you most?

15.title: On My Holy Mountain
15.context: The chapter's destination reverses its beginning: the God who refused consultation promises a second exodus, a wilderness of the peoples where He pleads His case face to face, and a mountain where the whole house serves Him in acceptance.
15.question: What would it mean for you to be brought out, judged face to face, and still end up accepted?

16.title: I Am Against You
16.context: After the complaint about parables, the next word comes without a picture: a drawn sword against Jerusalem that cuts off righteous and wicked together, and a prophet commanded to sigh with a breaking heart where the people can see.
16.question: What truth in your life needs to be said plainly now, without a story to soften it?

16.title: The Sword Song
16.context: The sword song is the book's most musical passage, built for chanting, with the blade sharpened for slaughter and polished to flash like lightning. Its refrain asks the hearers whether they can rejoice while the rod that disciplines is already swinging.
16.question: What celebration in your life is going on too close to a warning you can already hear?

16.title: The King at the Fork
16.context: Nebuchadnezzar pauses where the road divides between Rabbah of Ammon and Jerusalem, and works his divination in full: arrows shaken, household gods consulted, a liver examined. The lot that falls on Jerusalem is cast by a pagan king and stands as God's decision.
16.question: What decision are you waiting on that may already have been made by hands you do not respect?

16.title: Your Day Has Come, O Wicked Prince
16.context: The prince addressed is Zedekiah, though the oracle leaves him unnamed, a crown removed until the one comes to whom it rightfully belongs. Ruin, repeated three times, is the last word on the old kingship in this book.
16.question: What crown, title, role, control, are you holding past the day God has set for it to come off?

16.title: Ammon's Turn Will Come
16.context: Ammon escaped the fork in the road only by the lot falling elsewhere. Its false visions bought delay, not pardon, and the sword is promised a second drawing in Ammon's own land.
16.question: What consequence have you merely postponed, and what would repentance do with the delay?

17.title: Will You Judge the City of Bloodshed?
17.context: Chapter 22 is arranged as a court session: the prophet is appointed prosecutor of his own city, and the charges are read aloud so the defendant cannot claim ignorance. Two counts head the indictment, bloodshed and idols.
17.question: What charge, privately known, would you least want read aloud in your own hearing?

17.title: Down the Whole Social Order
17.context: The catalogue descends level by level, princes, households, lenders, judges, and finds the rot is not in one class but in the system. Bribes, interest, extortion, and forgotten God appear in the same breath.
17.question: Which level of your own world, home, work, church, do you exempt from the examination you apply to the others?

17.title: Dross in the Furnace
17.context: Dross is the scum skimmed off molten silver, the waste that looks like metal and is not. Jerusalem is pictured as a furnace charge of copper, tin, iron, and lead with the silver gone, precious in appearance and worthless in the melt.
17.question: What in your life has the look of the real thing and would not survive being melted down?

17.title: A Roll Call of Failed Guards
17.context: The third oracle names the offices one by one: prophets conspiring, priests blurring holy and common, officials like wolves, prophets whitewashing, and the people of the land practicing the extortion they learned from above.
17.question: Which guard post, in your family or work, has gone unmanned because everyone assumed someone else stood there?

17.title: I Searched for a Man
17.context: The wall Ezekiel was told to repair is a wall of standing people: one man in the breach, praying and holding the line, would have changed the outcome. The search is described in the past tense, and it found no one.
17.question: Where is the gap you already know about, and what has kept you from being the one standing in it?

18.title: Two Sisters Named
18.context: The names are the allegory's key: Oholah means her tent, for Samaria worshiped in a tent of her own making; Oholibah means my tent is in her, for God's tent stood in Jerusalem. The elder sister falls first, and the younger watches.
18.question: Which warning have you watched play out in someone else's life at close range?

18.title: Oholah and the Assyrians
18.context: Samaria's alliance with Assyria dressed itself as desire for its governors and horsemen, splendid in purple. The lover became the executioner: Assyria stripped the city, took her children, and ended her in 722 BC.
18.question: What protector in your life has the record of becoming a destroyer once it owned you?

18.title: Oholibah Saw This, and Went Further
18.context: The allegory's center is a comparison: the younger sister watched the elder's ruin in full detail and increased the corruption anyway, adding Babylon to the old Egyptian pattern. Knowledge, the chapter insists, is not the same as learning.
18.question: What have you seen clearly, consequence and all, and done anyway?

18.title: The Lovers Become the Mob
18.context: The guest list of the invasion is read like a summons: the very peoples she courted are incited against her from every side. Judgment in this chapter works by handing the sinner to her sin, dressed now as an army.
18.question: What habit promises you company and is quietly assembling your consequences?

18.title: Judged with the Sentence of Adulteresses
18.context: The chapter restarts as a courtroom, because the allegory is a legal case and not only a story. Child sacrifice is named in the indictment in plain words, and the sentence aims at an end of the pattern for every woman watching.
18.question: What in your history needs the courtroom treatment, plain charges and a verdict, rather than another retelling?

19.title: Write Down Today's Date
19.context: The date given, the ninth year, tenth month, tenth day, is the day Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem began, recorded identically in 2 Kings 25:1. Ezekiel, six hundred miles away, is told to date his notebook by it.
19.question: What date on your calendar marks a beginning you only understood much later?

19.title: The Rust in the Pot
19.context: The pot's rust, encrusted and unscrubbed, is the city's corruption made visible: what clings inside cannot be cooked out, only emptied out piece by piece and burned. The interpretation leaves the parable no room to stay a parable.
19.question: What has been clinging in your life that gradual improvement cannot reach?

19.title: The Desire of Your Eyes
19.context: Ezekiel's wife is never named in the book, and she speaks no recorded word; she exists in the text as the desire of his eyes. Her death in one evening, and his forbidden mourning, became the most costly sign act of his ministry.
19.question: What grief have you had to carry quietly because the role you were given left no room to show it?

19.title: Won't You Tell Us What This Means?
19.context: The exiles finally ask the question the sign acts were always fishing for. The answer binds the prophet's restraint to their future collapse: when the news comes, they will do as he did, and know the LORD by their own uncovered mouths.
19.question: Whose example, watched for years, explained itself to you in a single day?

19.title: The Day the Fugitive Comes
19.context: The promise is the loose thread the whole book will pull eight chapters later: a fugitive will arrive, and the silenced prophet's mouth will open. Until then, the sign stands uncompleted, and so does Ezekiel.
19.question: What promise are you holding whose fulfillment depends on news you cannot hurry?

20.title: Because Ammon Said Aha
20.context: Ammon was Judah's relative through Lot, and its whole recorded sin here is a sound: Aha, clapped hands and stamped feet over a neighbor's fall. The nations section opens by treating gloating as a crime worth a national sentence.
20.question: What sound, cheer, joke, shared headline, have you made over someone's ruin that you would not defend here?

20.title: Like All the Other Nations
20.context: Moab's sin is a sentence, not a cheer: that Judah is just like everyone else. The sneer denies there was ever anything distinct to lose, and it is answered by opening Moab's flank to the same desert raiders.
20.question: Where have you made peace with being indistinguishable, and what did it cost?

20.title: Edom Acted Vengefully
20.context: Edom's grudge ran back to twin brothers, Jacob and Esau, and forward through centuries of border war. This series met its full charge sheet in Obadiah; Ezekiel's oracle is the same sentence in a shorter docket.
20.question: What old family or church grudge have you inherited and kept paying on?

20.title: By the Hand of My People Israel
20.context: The executioner named for Edom is the twist: Israel itself, the brother nation Edom hunted, will one day carry out the sentence. History books outside the Bible record Judah's later domination of Edom in the centuries after the exile.
20.question: Whose hands have carried out a correction in your life that you never expected God to use?

20.title: An Old, Unrelenting Grudge
20.context: The Philistines, Israel's coastal enemy since the days of the judges, are charged not with invasion but with contempt nursed across generations. The nations oracles end where they began, with the heart's posture toward a neighbor's fall.
20.question: What contempt have you kept on retainer, available whenever a certain name comes up?

21.title: Aha, the Gate Is Broken
21.context: Tyre was an island fortress and the Mediterranean's great trading power, grown rich on the land routes that passed through Jerusalem. Her opening line treats a sister city's fall as a business opportunity.
21.question: What opportunity in your life opened only because someone else fell?

21.title: Walls Broken, Towers Down
21.context: Nebuchadnezzar is named as the first wave, though the oracle keeps saying they, as if more armies stand behind his. Tyre endured his siege for thirteen years, and the mainland city fell while the island held out.
21.question: What are you still holding out in, after the mainland of the matter has already fallen?

21.title: A Bare Rock for Spreading Nets
21.context: The end state is precise: not a ruin but a rock, scraped clean, useful only to fishermen drying nets. Centuries later Alexander the Great would throw Tyre's rubble into the sea to build his causeway to the island.
21.question: What would be left of your life's work if it were scraped down to the rock, and would the rock be honest?

21.title: The Princes of the Sea Come Down
21.context: The reaction shots belong to Tyre's trading partners, merchant princes who step down from their thrones to sit in mourning. Their lament is quoted as evidence: the whole sea economy knows what has been lost.
21.question: Who would sit down in the dirt at your fall, and what would their lament say you were?

21.title: Never to Be Found Again
21.context: The chapter closes with the sea itself doing the burying, the deep covering the city like the flood of the oldest stories. Sought but never found is the epitaph for a place that thought its position made it permanent.
21.question: What permanent thing in your life is actually a position, tides and all?

22.title: Take Up a Lament for Tyre
22.context: The lament is ordered before the fall it mourns, so the whole glorious inventory is read in the past tense of grief. Tyre's own self-description is quoted back to her: perfect in beauty, a ship whose builders made her so.
22.question: What would your life's inventory sound like read as a lament instead of a resume?

22.title: Rowers, Pilots, and Guards
22.context: The ship's crew list is a map of the known world: Sidon and Arvad row, Byblos caulks seams, Persia and Lydia and Put stand guard. Tyre's strength was hired, allied, and imported, magnificent and rented.
22.question: Which of your strengths are actually yours, and which are hired help that could be recalled?

22.title: The Manifest Read Aloud
22.context: The cargo list runs from Tarshish silver to Ethiopian ebony, with Judah and Israel themselves appearing as suppliers of wheat, honey, oil, and balm. The poem slows down on purpose: a mourner reads names one by one.
22.question: What names, of people, places, seasons, would a slow reading of your life pause over longest?

22.title: The East Wind Broke You
22.context: The wreck takes almost no verses after the long inventory: one wind, one breaking, and rowers, cargo, soldiers, and pilots go into the heart of the sea together. The ratio is the sermon, glory long and the fall short.
22.question: What east wind, one diagnosis, one letter, one call, could your current setup not survive?

22.title: On the Shore, Covered in Ashes
22.context: The closing scene is not the wreck but the watchers: captains on the shore throwing dust on their heads, and merchants hissing at a horror they cannot stop looking at. A great fall always has an audience, and the audience keeps trading.
22.question: When you watch someone else's wreck from the shore, what does it stir in you besides relief that it is not yours?

23.title: You Say, I Am a God
23.context: The ruler of Tyre is a step below the king of the next oracle: a working prince whose wisdom built real wealth, and whose heart converted the wealth into a claim of divinity. The charge is not that he failed, but that he succeeded and misread it.
23.question: Where has competence, yours or someone's, started dressing itself as something more than human?

23.title: Yet You Are a Man
23.context: The sentence imports the executioners Tyre most feared, foreigners, the most ruthless of nations, to prove the single point: the self-declared god will die the death of a man, at sea, by strangers' hands.
23.question: What proof would your pride least survive, and why that one?

23.title: The Seal of Perfection, in Eden
23.context: The lament for the king shifts registers into Eden, gemstones, and a guardian cherub on God's holy mountain, language that has made readers ask for two thousand years whether more than a king is in view. The book itself keeps the picture aimed at Tyre's king; the identification of the cherub with any other figure belongs to interpretation, and Christians have read it differently.
23.question: What splendor in your past, a season of real giftedness, has the longest shadow over your present humility?

23.title: Sidon, and the Thorn Removed
23.context: Sidon, Tyre's older sister city up the coast, receives a compact oracle of plague and blood, and the section around Israel begins to clear. The nations are being dealt with in a ring, nearest first and Egypt last.
23.question: What small, overlooked trouble near you keeps getting skipped because a bigger one is louder?

23.title: No More a Pricking Brier
23.context: The Tyre section ends not on a nation but on Israel's future quiet: the scornful neighbors gone, houses built, vineyards planted, secure dwelling. It is the first fully peaceful paragraph in seven chapters of oracles.
23.question: What would secure dwelling look like for you, concretely, street and table and door?

24.title: The Great Monster in the Nile
24.context: Pharaoh is pictured as the Nile's crocodile-like monster, claiming the river as his own creation and possession. Egypt's kings had leaned on that river, and Israel's kings had leaned on Egypt, for centuries by this point.
24.question: What river, resource, system, person, do you speak of as mine in a way that leaves God out?

24.title: Hooks in Your Jaws
24.context: The monster is fished, not fought: hooks, a haul onto the bank, and the river's fish stuck to his scales dying with him in the open field. Egypt's fall will strand every smaller thing that attached itself to her strength.
24.question: What have you attached yourself to that would strand you if it were hauled out?

24.title: A Desolate Waste for Forty Years
24.context: The sentence carries a map and a number: from Migdol in the north to Aswan in the south, forty years of desolation, and a return to a humbled, lowly kingdom that will never rule nations again or be trusted as a reed staff by Israel.
24.question: What has God humbled in your life permanently, and what did the humbling make possible?

24.title: The Twenty-Seventh Year
24.context: This oracle is dated later than any other in the book, 571 BC, and it handles an embarrassment honestly: Babylon's thirteen-year siege of Tyre paid its army nothing, so Egypt is assigned as the wages. Prophecy here keeps books.
24.question: What long labor of yours went unpaid, and where might God be assigning the wages from an unexpected direction?

24.title: A Horn for the House of Israel
24.context: The chapter's last verse ties Egypt's fall to two Israelite events: a horn, a budding of strength, for God's people, and Ezekiel's mouth opened among them. The prophet's silence is scheduled to end inside history, not outside it.
24.question: What strength is quietly budding in your life while the loud powers get the attention?

25.title: A Day of Clouds
25.context: The day of the LORD, this book's name for God's settled appointment with nations, comes for Egypt as a day of clouds, the gloom Ezekiel used for Gog's invasion as well. Ethiopia, Libya, and Lydia fall in the same shadow, allies included.
25.question: What appointment are you treating as weather, hoping it passes, that is actually on the calendar?

25.title: Fire in Egypt, News on the Water
25.context: Messengers in swift boats carry the news down to unsuspecting Ethiopia, panic traveling the Nile faster than the army. The oracle lingers on the spread of the word, because dread is part of the sentence.
25.question: What news are you dreading the arrival of, and what would readiness actually look like?

25.title: City by City
25.context: The roll of cities, Memphis, Thebes, Zoan, Pathros, reads like Egypt's own hall of fame receiving sentences one by one. No place in the list is too storied or too sacred to be named.
25.question: What in your life have you assumed was exempt by reputation, age, or past usefulness?

25.title: The Arm Already Broken
25.context: This oracle is dated in the eleventh year, when Pharaoh's army had already been beaten back from Jerusalem's siege once. The arm image is surgical: broken, unbound, too weak to hold a sword, while Babylon's arm is strengthened in the same sentence.
25.question: What strength of yours is not injured but finished, and what have you been splinting instead of admitting it?

25.title: Scattered Among the Nations
25.context: The chapter closes by handing Egypt Israel's own sentence, dispersion among the nations and countries. The formula is deliberate: the reed staff Israel leaned on receives the exact judgment of the people who leaned.
25.question: Where have you and the thing you trusted ended up sharing the same consequence?

26.title: Look at Assyria, a Cedar in Lebanon
26.context: To explain Egypt, the prophet is told to tell Pharaoh about a tree already fallen: Assyria, the empire Babylon had destroyed a generation earlier. The cedar's shade housed nations like birds and beasts under a canopy.
26.question: Whose fallen example is close enough to your situation to be a real warning, if you let it?

26.title: Delivered to the Ruthless
26.context: The cedar's fall is laid to one cause, its heart was proud of its height, and its purpose in falling is stated: so that no tree by the waters will exalt itself again. The tallest thing in the garden becomes the garden's lesson.
26.question: What height, in skill, reputation, or certainty, is your heart most proud of?

26.title: The Pit Receives Another
26.context: When the cedar went down, God Himself caused the mourning and comforted the trees of Eden already in the Pit with fresh company. The underworld in this poem is a leveling place where empires lie down together.
26.question: What company does your ambition keep that your conscience would not choose?

26.title: Like a Monster in the Seas
26.context: The last Egypt oracle is dated in the twelfth year and opens by merging Pharaoh's two portraits, lion among the nations and monster thrashing the waters foul. A net, drawn by many peoples, ends what no single hunter could.
26.question: What pattern in your life has two faces depending on who is watching, lion here, monster there?

26.title: The Tour of the Pit
26.context: The closing roll is a guided walk past the graves of Assyria, Elam, Meshek, Tubal, Edom, and Sidon, each with its terror spent and its honor gone. Pharaoh's only consolation is company: he will see them all and lie down among them.
26.question: If your life were summarized in one line on such a roll, what would you want the line to be unable to say?

27.title: The Watchman Charter, Again
27.context: The book's second half opens by repeating the commission of chapter 3 almost word for word. What has changed is not the charter but the moment: the sword the watchman was posted to watch for has now fallen on the city.
27.question: What duty in your life needs to be taken up again in a new season, in nearly the same words as the first time?

27.title: I Take No Pleasure
27.context: The exiles' new saying is despair, our offenses weigh us down, and God's answer repeats chapter 18's oath with the volume up: turn and live. Past righteousness will not shield present sin, and past sin will not bar present repentance.
27.question: Which direction are you currently walking, and what would the first turn actually consist of?

27.title: The City Has Been Taken
27.context: The fugitive arrives in the twelfth year, months after the fall by the Babylonian calendar, walking the whole refugee road. The night before he came, Ezekiel's mouth was opened, ending a silence that had lasted, in its full form, about seven years.
27.question: What have you waited to say until a particular piece of news arrived?

27.title: Abraham Was Only One Man
27.context: Back in the ruins, survivors argue from Abraham's inheritance while living on blood-eating, idolatry, and violence. The answer takes their premise and reverses it: if one righteous man inherited, what should many wicked ones expect?
27.question: What inheritance, spiritual, family, national, are you claiming by descent while living against its terms?

27.title: A Lovely Song, Nothing More
27.context: The chapter closes on the audience Ezekiel actually has: people who invite each other to hear the word the way they would attend a singer, enjoy the performance, and practice none of it. When it comes to pass, the last verse says, they will know a prophet was among them.
27.question: What truth have you applauded that you have not yet obeyed?

28.title: Shepherds Who Feed Themselves
28.context: With the kings gone, the audit widens to every leader who drew wages from the flock: kings, officials, priests, the whole shepherd class. The charges are pastoral accounting, milk taken, wool worn, the fat slaughtered, and the weak, sick, injured, strayed, and lost unvisited.
28.question: Whose care has been assigned to you, and what have you taken from them instead?

28.title: Scattered for Lack of a Shepherd
28.context: The flock's condition is written as the shepherds' report card: scattered on the mountains, food for wild animals, wandered and unsearched-for. God then names Himself the shepherds' opponent, which no failed officeholder in the book survives.
28.question: Who has wandered off from your care, and have you searched, or only noticed?

28.title: I Myself Will Search
28.context: The sentence the chapter exists for is spoken in the first person thirteen times over: I will search, seek, rescue, gather, feed, and bind up. The search is pictured across countries and peoples, on a cloudy and dark day, like the one just past.
28.question: What have you lost, a person, a part of yourself, a calling, that you need God to search for because you cannot?

28.title: Judgment Between Sheep and Sheep
28.context: The flock itself is also judged: fat sheep and strong rams have fouled the pasture and water for the lean, butting the weak aside. Restoration is not a blanket amnesty; the rescued community gets a referee who saves the lean sheep from the strong.
28.question: Where have you been the strong sheep at someone else's pasture or water?

28.title: One Shepherd, a Covenant of Peace
28.context: The office is restaffed with a figure the book has now promised three ways: the tender sprig, the prince to come, and here My servant David, one shepherd over a reunited flock under a covenant of peace, with showers of blessing in season. Christians have long read this shepherd as pointing beyond any earthly king, a reading the details here invite but do not settle.
28.question: What would peace, in the concrete sense of safety, food, and quiet, change about your daily life first?

29.title: Set Your Face Against Mount Seir
29.context: Edom gets a second, fuller oracle here, after the short one in chapter 25, because its sin at the fall is not finished being answered. The mountain country of Seir is sentenced to the desolation it celebrated in Judah.
29.question: What old matter in your life keeps returning because it was never fully answered the first time?

29.title: These Two Lands Will Be Mine
29.context: The boast God answers is a property claim made over emptied land: the two nations, Israel and Judah, will be Edom's possession. It was spoken, the oracle says, while the LORD was there, present in the land Edom thought abandoned.
29.question: What have you claimed, in words or plans, on the assumption that God had vacated the premises?

29.title: While the Whole Earth Rejoices
29.context: The measure-for-measure ending is almost festive: Edom's desolation is scheduled for the day of everyone else's joy. Judgment in Ezekiel is rarely private; whole landscapes rejoice or mourn together in these poems.
29.question: Whose joy has ever felt like your loss, and what does that feeling confess?

29.title: Mountains That Will Shoot Out Branches
29.context: The address changes from Seir to Israel's mountains, spoken to directly, as if the land had ears and a long memory of insult. The promise is agricultural first: branches, fruit, tilled fields, and people soon to return.
29.question: What ground in your life, a place, a practice, a relationship, is God promising to make fruitful again?

29.title: Better Than at the Beginning
29.context: Read side by side, the two oracles are one sermon with two addresses: the mountain that gloated becomes desert, and the mountains that were mocked become gardens. The nations are promised they will hear the difference.
29.question: Where would you most like to be able to say, God treated me better in the end than at the beginning?

30.title: The Land Defiled, the Name Profaned
30.context: The promise begins with a review that flatters no one: Israel defiled the land like ceremonial uncleanness, was scattered for bloodshed and idols, and then profaned God's name among the nations precisely by being His exiled people.
30.question: What has your worst season made people conclude about the God you belong to?

30.title: Not for Your Sake
30.context: Twice in three verses the motive is declared, so it cannot be missed: the restoration is for the sake of God's holy name, not Israel's deserving. Grace here is not God overlooking the record but acting on a different basis altogether.
30.question: What good thing are you still trying to deserve that God may only ever give for His own reasons?

30.title: Clean Water, a New Heart
30.context: The sequence is all first-person verbs: gather, sprinkle clean water, cleanse, give a new heart, remove the stone, put in His Spirit, and cause obedience. Israel contributes nothing to the list but the need for every item on it.
30.question: Which item in that sequence, cleansing, a new heart, the Spirit within, do you most need to ask for by name?

30.title: Then You Will Remember
30.context: The people's part comes last and is memory, not achievement: saved first, they will remember their ways and loathe themselves for them. In this book, repentance is what grace feels like from the inside, afterward.
30.question: What memory of your past now produces gratitude for rescue instead of only shame?

30.title: Like the Garden of Eden
30.context: The results are visible from the road: ruined cities resettled, waste land tilled until passersby compare it to Eden, and a people multiplied like a flock at festival time. Ezekiel is told to let the house ask for it, as if the promise waits on prayer.
30.question: What restored place in your life would make a passerby stop and ask what happened there?

31.title: Can These Bones Live?
31.context: The valley vision is the book's most famous scene, and it begins with a survey: the bones are very many and very dry, long past any natural hope. Ezekiel's answer to God's question is the book's most careful sentence: only You know.
31.question: What in your life is past the very dry stage, where honesty requires Ezekiel's answer instead of optimism?

31.title: Prophesy to the Bones
31.context: The answer to the question is a task, not an explanation: preach to the bones. Breath, sinews, flesh, and skin are promised in order, and the bones are addressed as hearers of the word of the LORD before they are anything else.
31.question: What dead thing in front of you needs to be spoken to in God's name rather than merely assessed?

31.title: Prophesy to the Breath
31.context: The first sermon produces a body that still has no breath, and a second sermon is required, addressed to the wind itself, from the four winds. The army stands only when both words have been spoken: structure and Spirit, in that order.
31.question: Where do you have the form of a thing, assembled and correct, still waiting for breath?

31.title: These Bones Are the Whole House
31.context: God interprets His own vision and names the discouragement beneath it: the exiles say their hope is gone and they are cut off. The graves that will open are exile's graves, and the land they will enter is their own.
31.question: Whose voice speaks the sentence our hope is gone in your house, and what has God already said against it?

31.title: I Will Put My Spirit in You
31.context: The book is careful about the picture's limits, and a faithful reading keeps them: the text's own interpretation is national restoration, life in the land under God's Spirit. Readers through the centuries, including the New Testament's resurrection hope, have heard more in it, and the two hearings need not fight.
31.question: Where do you need resurrection to mean first what it meant to its first hearers, before it means more?

32.title: Take a Single Stick and Write
32.context: The last sign act is performed with a pen, on two sticks or tablets inscribed for Judah and for Joseph. The prophet joins them in one hand, where the crowd can see there is no seam left to run a finger along.
32.question: What two parts of your life, your people, your church, are you holding in separate hands that God means as one?

32.title: I Will Make Them One Nation
32.context: The explanation begins with God's own hand doing what the prophet's pictured: gathering from every side, one nation on the mountains of Israel, one king, never again two. The division had stood since Solomon's death, some four centuries by then.
32.question: What long division, older than anyone living, have you stopped expecting God to heal?

32.title: They Will No Longer Defile Themselves
32.context: The union has a holiness condition built into it, or rather out of it: the idols and detestable things that split the kingdom are gone from the picture, because the Savior saves them from all their dwelling places of sin at once.
32.question: What would unity cost you in the specific habits that keep your side separate?

32.title: My Servant David, Their Prince Forever
32.context: The shepherd promised in chapter 34 is named here without apology, David, as king over the united nation, under an everlasting covenant of peace, with God's sanctuary in their midst forever. The book means the permanence literally, whatever readers conclude about the timetable.
32.question: Whose leadership would you follow into permanent peace, and what makes you trust it?

32.title: The Nations Will Know I Sanctify Israel
32.context: The oracle ends where the whole movement has been heading: my dwelling place with them, I will be their God, and the nations reading the arrangement correctly. Presence, not power, is the restoration's final proof.
32.question: What evidence of God's dwelling would the watching people around you actually be able to see?

33.title: Set Your Face Against Gog
33.context: Gog, of the land of Magog, chief prince of Meshek and Tubal, arrives with a coalition named from the edges of Ezekiel's world, Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, Beth Togarmah. Readers have proposed identifications for Gog in every century, and the book itself supplies none beyond his title, direction, and end.
33.question: How do you hold a prophecy whose details you cannot pin down without either forcing them or discarding them?

33.title: In the Latter Years
33.context: The timing is insisted on twice: the invasion comes after the restoration, against a land recovered from war and a people gathered and dwelling securely. Gog is drawn up like a cloud covering a land at rest, not a land in ruins.
33.question: What good season in your life has it seemed hardest to believe could be interrupted?

33.title: An Evil Plan of Plunder
33.context: Gog's motive is given in his own interior planning, and it is pure plunder: unwalled villages, quiet people, livestock and possessions. Even the trading nations in the poem ask the question the reader is asking, have you come to seize spoil, as if the motive is too small for the army.
33.question: What small motive have you dressed in large machinery, yours or someone else's?

33.title: That the Nations May Know Me
33.context: God's motive is stated as plainly as Gog's: the invasion is brought, in the latter days, so that the nations may know Him when He is sanctified through Gog before their eyes. The enemy is, without knowing it, an exhibit in someone else's demonstration.
33.question: Where might God be using opposition in your life as an exhibit of something larger than the fight?

33.title: Fury, Earthquake, and Hail
33.context: The battle is fought entirely by God, in earthquake, plague, torrential rain, hailstones, fire, and the invaders' own swords turning on each other. Israel fires no shot in the chapter; the security that attracted the invasion is defended by its Giver.
33.question: What battle have you been preparing to fight that may not be yours to fight at all?

34.title: I Will Strike the Bow from Your Hand
34.context: Chapter 39 retells the invasion from the far side, as accomplished fact, and opens with the disarming: bow struck from the left hand, arrows from the right. Gog falls on the mountains of Israel with his hordes, given to the birds and beasts.
34.question: What weapon, argument, leverage, habit, would change everything if it were simply struck out of your hand?

34.title: Seven Years, Seven Months
34.context: The cleanup is the oracle's strangest arithmetic: seven years burning captured weapons for fuel, and seven months burying the dead to cleanse the land, with a valley renamed for the multitude buried there. Victory in this book ends in sanitation crews, not parades.
34.question: What long, unglamorous cleanup has a victory in your life required afterward?

34.title: A Sacrificial Feast for the Birds
34.context: God hosts the banquet Himself, calling every bird and beast to eat the flesh of princes and warriors as at a sacrifice. The image is deliberately shocking: the invaders who came to plunder a feast become one.
34.question: What tables have you set, plans, ambitions, appetites, that could end by consuming the setter?

34.title: The Nations Will See
34.context: The lesson runs in both directions: the nations learn that Israel's exile was for Israel's sin, not God's weakness, and Israel learns the same history from the other side. A misread catastrophe is publicly reinterpreted.
34.question: What event in your life do onlookers explain wrongly, and what is the truer reading?

34.title: I Will Hide My Face No Longer
34.context: The restoration movement ends with the book's fullest promise chain: Jacob restored, mercy on the whole house, forgotten shame, the Spirit poured out, and God's face never hidden again. It is the sentence the glory's return in chapter 43 will perform.
34.question: What would it mean, practically, for God to hide His face from your life no longer?

35.title: The Twenty-Fifth Year
35.context: The vision is dated twice over, the twenty-fifth year of exile and the fourteenth after the city's fall, about 573 BC. The guide is a man whose appearance is like bronze, carrying a linen cord and a measuring reed some ten feet long.
35.question: What date in your life carries two meanings at once, an exile year and an after year?

35.title: The Wall and the East Gate
35.context: The tour starts outside with a wall, one reed thick and one reed high, and gives the east gatehouse more verses than the sanctuary itself. Gates, thresholds, guardrooms, and steps are the vision's native language.
35.question: Why do you think God, in this vision, measures the approaches before He measures the house?

35.title: Climbing by Sevens and Eights
35.context: The inner gates have eight steps where the outer have seven, so the whole tour is an ascent in number as well as holiness. Courts, chambers for the singers and priests, and the temple porch are paced off one measurement at a time.
35.question: Where does your life need measuring, plain and unhurried, before it needs anything else?

35.title: The House Itself
35.context: Chapter 41 measures the sanctuary: the outer room forty cubits, the Most Holy Place twenty square, side chambers in three stories, carved cherubim and palm trees, each cherub with the face of a man and the face of a lion.
35.question: What is the most holy place in your life, and what have you built around it to protect it?

35.title: The Priests' Chambers and the Outer Wall
35.context: The buildings finish with the priests' eating and changing chambers, holy garments kept apart from common use. The tour ends at a wall five hundred cubits square whose stated purpose is separation between the holy and the common.
35.question: What separation, between the holy and the common, has gone blurry in your routines?

36.title: The Sound of Rushing Waters
36.context: The glory returns by the road it left, from the east, with a voice like the roar of many waters and the earth shining from its splendor. Ezekiel names it as the same vision he saw at the Kebar and at the city's destruction, and falls on his face a third time.
36.question: What has God brought back into your life by the same road it left?

36.title: The Temple Filled
36.context: The entry is precise about the door: in through the east gate, the gate of the departure, and the glory fills the house while the prophet watches from the inner court. Chapter 10's threshold scene is run in reverse.
36.question: What door in your life stands open to return, and what would filling look like on the other side of it?

36.title: The Place of My Throne
36.context: The voice speaks from inside the house and names the terms: the place of My throne, no more defilement by the old palace-burial intimacy, and the kings' memorials removed. The old closeness of crown and altar is treated as part of the sin.
36.question: What closeness in your life, to power, to a person, to a habit, has been defilement dressed as intimacy?

36.title: Describe the Temple, That They May Be Ashamed
36.context: The purpose of nine chapters of measurement is finally stated, and it is not architectural: the design is a mirror, shown so the house will be ashamed of its iniquities and measure itself against the plan. Fulfillment of the vision, literal, spiritual, or both, has been read differently by faithful readers for centuries.
36.question: What vision of what your life could be has ever produced the right kind of shame in you, the kind that moves?

36.title: The Altar in Tiers
36.context: The chapter ends with the law of the temple, absolute holiness on the mountain's top, and the altar measured tier by tier, then consecrated with seven days of offerings. The vision's God attends to gutters, ledges, and steps with the same care as thrones.
36.question: What small, unglamorous part of your service needs the same careful measuring as the great parts?

37.title: The Gate That Stays Shut
37.context: The east outer gate is sealed permanently, not as a ruin but as a memorial: the LORD has entered through it. Only the prince may sit inside its gateway, and only to eat bread before the LORD.
37.question: What has God closed in your life that is meant to stay closed, as a memorial rather than a loss?

37.title: An Audit of the Old Priesthood
37.context: The chapter audits the old order before staffing the new: Levites who strayed after idols are demoted to gatekeepers and butchers, bearing their shame in reduced service, while the ministry near God's person is reserved.
37.question: What demotion, of role, trust, or access, has your own wandering honestly earned, and how do you carry it?

37.title: The Sons of Zadok Who Kept the Charge
37.context: Zadok was David's priest, and his line is set apart here for one recorded reason: they kept the charge of the sanctuary when Israel went astray. Their reward is proximity, to come near, stand before God, and offer.
37.question: Who kept the charge, quietly and unfashionably, in a season when everyone around them wandered?

37.title: Linen, Not Wool
37.context: The working code is a series of distinctions: linen that does not sweat, hair neither shaved nor wild, no wine on duty, marriages and mourning fenced, and the priest's core teaching job stated, to show the people the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean.
37.question: Which distinction, holy or common, clean or unclean, rest or duty, has blurred most in your current week?

37.title: I Am Their Inheritance
37.context: The priests' pay is the chapter's last word and it is a person, not land: I am their inheritance, I am their possession. The firstfruits and devoted things that feed them all arrive because God, not an estate, is their portion.
37.question: What would have to be true for you to say, and mean, that God Himself is your portion?

38.title: The Sacred District
38.context: Chapters 45 and 46 draw the country around the sanctuary like a constitution: a sacred allotment for sanctuary and priests, a strip for the Levites, land for the city, and the prince's portion on both sides, fenced in by design against expansion.
38.question: What fences would you build now, while you are thinking clearly, against your own future overreach?

38.title: Enough, O Princes
38.context: The address to the office is a rebuke aimed backward across the whole monarchy: enough violence and robbery, honest scales, honest measures, honest weights. Land reform in this vision begins with the measuring tools themselves.
38.question: Where do your scales, time, money, credit, need a recalibration that only honesty can perform?

38.title: The Prince Provides the Offerings
38.context: The prince's job description is liturgical and financial rather than military: he funds and supplies the feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths from the people's contributions, so that worship runs on provision instead of plunder. The calendar given runs through the appointed feasts of the year.
38.question: What does your leadership, at home or work, mostly fund and supply, and what does that say it is for?

38.title: The Weekly Rhythm
38.context: Chapter 46 gives the week its shape: the inner court's east gate shut six working days, opened on the Sabbath and the New Moon, with the prince entering by its porch and the people worshiping at its doorway. Ordinary people, this chapter says, leave by the opposite gate from the one they entered, a small law against retracing.
38.question: What rhythm of shut and open gates orders your week, and who set it?

38.title: The Prince Must Not Take
38.context: The closing laws protect the small landowner from the throne: a prince's gift to a son stays his, gifts to servants revert in the year of liberty, and no prince may seize a family's inheritance by force. The vision's final protection is aimed at the memory of Naboth's vineyard and every king who coveted one.
38.question: What is one thing that belongs to someone weaker than you that your power, mood, or convenience must never touch?

39.title: A Trickle from the Threshold
39.context: The tour's last wonder begins almost invisibly: water seeping from under the temple's threshold, south of the altar, out through the gatehouse. Nothing else in the nine chapters grows; this alone increases.
39.question: What has God started in your life as a trickle you nearly stepped over?

39.title: Ankles, Knees, Waist, Over the Head
39.context: The measuring resumes, but this time the thing measured outgrows the reed: a thousand cubits to the ankles, another to the knees, another to the waist, and a fourth into a river no one can cross. Ezekiel is led through the first three and only watches the fourth.
39.question: Where is God leading you through water that gets deeper by His measurement, not your accident?

39.title: Water That Makes Everything Live
39.context: The river runs to the Arabah and into the Dead Sea, the saltiest water on earth, and freshens it until fishermen stand where nothing lived. The vision's claim is maximal: wherever the river flows, everything will live.
39.question: What dead sea in your world, a relationship, a place, a habit of heart, have you written off as unhealable?

39.title: The Swamps Left to Salt
39.context: The vision keeps one honest exception, because Ezekiel's promises never airbrush: the marshes at the sea's edge will not be healed, and are left for salt. Not everything adjacent to grace takes the healing, and the text says so without explaining.
39.question: What exception, near you and unhealed, do you need to acknowledge without letting it cancel the river?

39.title: Trees for Food, Leaves for Healing
39.context: The trees on the banks fruit every month, because their water flows from the sanctuary, and their leaves are for healing. The river answers the book's first vision: by the Kebar, glory stood over exiles; from the temple, life runs out to the deadest place on the map.
39.question: What flows out of your life, measurably, because it first flowed from God's presence into it?

40.title: These Are the Boundaries
40.context: The book ends with a land survey, borders paced off by named places, Joseph given two portions for his two tribes. Boundaries in this book are never red tape; they are how inheritance becomes real instead of rhetorical.
40.question: What boundary in your life is actually a form of God's generosity, marking what is yours to tend?

40.title: The Foreigner Inherits Beside You
40.context: Inside the survey sits the book's most startling clause: resident foreigners who have children in the land are to be treated as native-born and allotted an inheritance among the tribes. In a book preoccupied with separating holy from common, the line of belonging is drawn at dwelling and children, not blood.
40.question: Who is dwelling alongside your people, long and fruitfully, whom your categories still keep outside the inheritance?

40.title: Seven Tribes Across the North
40.context: Chapter 48 lays the tribal bands down in parallel strips from north to south, with the sacred portion, the city, and the prince's land at the center. The names are the old names, all twelve, including tribes lost to history for eight centuries by then.
40.question: What name from your people's past, written off for generations, do you believe God still has on His list?

40.title: The City Measured Last
40.context: The city is measured last and made perfectly square, 4,500 cubits a side, with three gates per side named for the tribes. Everyone's name is on a gate; the whole nation passes through its own names to get home.
40.question: Whose name would you put on a gate of the place you call home, and why theirs?

40.title: The LORD Is There
40.context: The last verse gives the city its new name, and the name is the book's whole journey in four words: from glory departed to glory returned, the place is no longer called forsaken or destroyed but simply noted for Who is in it. The perimeter is measured first, 18,000 cubits, and then the name is spoken over it.
40.question: If your life could be renamed for one true thing about God, what name would you hope it earned?
